title: Two Baskets of Figs
summary: After the first deportation to Babylon in 597 BC, the LORD shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs in front of the temple, one very good and one too rotten to eat. The good figs stand for the exiles already taken to Babylon, whom God will watch over, bring home, and give a new heart. The bad figs stand for King Zedekiah and those who remained in Jerusalem or were living in Egypt, who face sword, famine, and plague.
story: Jerusalem has now suffered its first great blow. Jehoiachin (here Jeconiah), the young king condemned in 22:24-30, has been carried off with the court and the skilled workers. Those left behind could easily conclude that they were the lucky ones, the faithful remnant God had spared, and that the exiles were the ones under judgment. This short vision turns that assumption upside down. The future of God's people lies with the exiles, not with the city. The chapter prepares for the letter to the exiles in chapter 29, and its promise of a heart to know God points ahead to the new covenant of chapter 31.
historical:
Verse 1 dates the vision precisely: after Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon from 605 to 562 BC, carried away Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim. This was the deportation of 597 BC, which 2 Kings 24:10-17 describes. Babylon took the king, his mother, his officials, the leading men, and the craftsmen and smiths, the people who could make weapons and organize resistance. Among them, according to Ezekiel 1:1-3, was the priest Ezekiel. Nebuchadnezzar installed Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah as king and renamed him Zedekiah. The Babylonian Chronicle, a cuneiform record of the period, independently notes Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Jerusalem in early 597 BC and his appointment of a new king of his own choosing.

Verse 8 also mentions Judeans “living in the land of Egypt.” Some had gone there earlier (Pharaoh Neco took King Jehoahaz to Egypt in 609 BC, 2 Kings 23:34), and many more would flee there after Jerusalem fell, as chapters 42 to 44 recount.
cultural:
Figs were one of the staple foods of the land, eaten fresh, dried, and pressed into cakes. The first figs of the season, ripening in early summer, were prized as a delicacy (Isaiah 28:4 and Hosea 9:10 use them as a picture of something eagerly desired). Baskets placed in front of the temple suggest offerings of firstfruits, which the law commanded Israel to bring to the sanctuary. A basket of rotten figs at the temple would be an offense: nothing fit to offer, nothing fit to eat.

The people in Jerusalem after 597 thought of themselves as the heirs of the land. Ezekiel reports the same attitude from the other side of the exile, with the Jerusalemites telling the deportees that they had gone far from the LORD and the land was now given to those who stayed (Ezekiel 11:15). In a culture that tied God's favor to possession of the land and access to the temple, Jeremiah's message was scandalous.
literary: This is a vision report, a form Jeremiah used at the start of his book (the almond branch and the boiling pot in 1:11-16). The pattern is the same: the LORD shows the prophet something, asks “what do you see?”, and then explains its meaning. The chapter is built as a simple contrast, with good figs and bad figs in verses 2 and 3, good exiles in verses 5 to 7, and bad remnant in verses 8 to 10. The language of verse 6 deliberately echoes Jeremiah's call in 1:10, where he was appointed to uproot and tear down, to build and to plant. Here the building and planting side of that commission comes into view.

outline.t: The vision: two baskets of figs before the temple
The good figs: the exiles, whom God will restore
The bad figs: Zedekiah and those who remained

doctrines.note: The exiles are not called good because they were better people; they had shared in the nation's sin. God regards them as good and commits himself to them: he will keep his eyes on them, return them, build and plant them, and give them a heart to know him. Their future rests on his initiative.

Verse 7 repeats the heart of the covenant formula, “They will be My people, and I will be their God.” The relationship the nation broke will be restored, and God himself will supply the inner change that makes it possible.
Those who clung to the city and the throne as proof of God's favor are the ones who will be scattered. Judgment falls on the false confidence that treated the temple and the land as guarantees.

words.note: Te'enah, fig or fig tree. The fig was a symbol of settled peace in Israel, with every man under his own vine and fig tree (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4). Figs appear eight times in this short chapter, so the image carries the whole message.

Galut, captivity or exile, used here collectively for the exiled community. The word would become one of the defining terms of Jewish history. Jeremiah's startling claim is that God's hope for his people now lives with the galut.

Yada, to know. In the Old Testament knowing God means more than holding correct information; it includes relationship, loyalty, and obedience. The promise of “a heart to know Me” in verse 7 anticipates the new covenant, where all will know the LORD (31:34).

christ: The promise that God will give his people a heart to know him is one Jeremiah develops in 31:31-34, which Hebrews 8 quotes as fulfilled in the new covenant Jesus brings. There is also a pattern here that the New Testament picks up: God's renewal comes to people who have lost everything the world counts as security, not to those who hold on to it. Jesus' blessing on the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3) and his warning that the first will be last run along the same line. Jesus himself used a fig tree as a sign of judgment on a fruitless temple establishment (Mark 11:12-21), which may echo prophetic images like this one, though the Gospels do not cite this chapter directly.

hard.q: Is God simply playing favorites, blessing one group and cursing another?
hard.a: It can look that way, and the chapter gives no moral scorecard showing that the exiles deserved better. Some readers see here a pure act of grace: God chooses to make a new beginning with people who have already been through judgment. Others note that the bad figs are marked by their response, since Zedekiah and his officials went on resisting God's word through Jeremiah (chapters 37 to 38) while the exiles were called to accept what had happened and seek God in Babylon (chapter 29). Both points belong together. The good figs are good because God regards them so and promises to change their hearts, and the bad figs are rejected for a persistent refusal the rest of the book documents. The chapter is also a warning against reading circumstances as proof of God's favor: those who seemed spared were in greater danger.

questions: The people who stayed in Jerusalem took their safety as proof that God was pleased with them. Where are you tempted to read comfort as approval?
Verse 7 says God will give his people a heart to know him. What is the difference between knowing about God and knowing him in the sense this chapter means?
How might this vision have sounded to someone who had just lost home and homeland in the deportation of 597 BC?
